article.title: Craniofacial Skeletal and Dentoalveolar Morphology in Bruxism: A Systematic Review of Imaging-Based and Morphometric Observational Studies.
article.authors: Buzatu R, Bumbu BA, Buzatu BLR
article.abstract: Background/Objectives: This systematic review evaluated whether craniofacial skeletal, mandibular and dentoalveolar morphology differs between individuals with and without bruxism. Methods: The protocol was prospectively registered (Open Science Framework) and the review follows PRISMA 2020. MEDLINE (PubMed) was searched from inception to 1 September 2026, supplemented by web, directory, reference-list and forward-citation searches; no other bibliographic database was searched. Two reviewers independently screened records and appraised quality with the JBI checklist. Because heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis, findings were synthesised narratively, with an exploratory effect-direction synthesis for the gonial angle stratified by diagnostic grade, age, temporomandibular disorder status and confounder control. Results: Sixteen studies (1387 participants, ten countries) were included; two used instrumental (definite) bruxism assessment. No consistent association was found with sagittal or vertical skeletal pattern, facial type or headform. Three adult imaging studies with non-instrumental diagnosis reported smaller gonial angles in bruxers (approximately 4° in two), and a fourth reported a reduction confined to women; no reduction was observed in either instrumental study or in any study with age-comparable groups not selected for temporomandibular disorder. Dentoalveolar findings were isolated and inconsistent. Conclusions: The evidence is insufficient to establish a characteristic craniofacial pattern or a reproducible gonial-angle association in bruxism; the reported differences are vulnerable to diagnostic misclassification and confounding. Craniofacial morphology alone should not be used to diagnose bruxism or to guide treatment decisions.
